A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DES framework by the same authors, despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added content to be matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original diffusion-model defense experiments, image-quality measurements, inpainting evaluations, ablations, and embedding analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on newer diffusion models, additional concepts, adaptive attacks, and benign-prompt semantic preservation.

M1.justification: The core target-generation procedure, three losses, and Algorithms 1–2 remain equivalent after notation changes. Limited extensions include concept-specific neutralization targets, independently training multiple text encoders, and optional DES combinations with filtering or negative prompts (Sections 4.1 and 4.4; Appendix B.7).

E1.justification: v2 adds training with 8,931 violence/illegal CoPro prompt pairs and 1,600 generated Van Gogh prompts. Section 4.4 evaluates six nonsexual I2P categories and Van Gogh concept erasure, substantially extending the represented content and tasks. I2P sexual-content evaluation and inpainting already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds GLoCE and Microsoft/OpenAI filters to SDv1.5 comparisons, EraseAnything to FLUX.1 comparisons, and string-filtering and negative-prompt baselines. FMN and SLD-medium disappear from corresponding sexual-content quantitative comparisons, although FMN remains in the new Van Gogh experiment.

E3.justification: v2 adds FLUX.1, SDXL, SDv3, and SDv3.5 configurations, CCE adaptive attacks, body-part detection counts, and PickScore, ImageReward, and BLIPScore evaluations. Its main black-box ASR average excludes I2P and therefore covers four attacks instead of five. Appendix E.1 additionally evaluates COCO subsets defined by their proximity to the nudity embedding.

E4.justification: Existing loss-component, loss-adjustment, coefficient, target-selection, embedding, and failure-case analyses largely survive under new locations or names. New analyses test whether basic defenses complement DES (Appendix B.7), scaling-factor sensitivity for other concepts (C.3.1), and semantic damage to benign prompts near and far from nudity, including individual cases (E.1). These substantially broaden the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard deviations across attack sets rather than uncertainty across repeated runs. Neither supplies seed counts, repeated-run estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's checklist explicitly acknowledges absent error bars but introduces no uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: New results include DES's 5.76% CCE ASR (Table 3), 1.88% mean ASR across six other NSFW categories (Table 5), and 9.47% five-set FLUX.1 ASR (Table 7). The four shared SDv1.5 DES attack scores remain unchanged; the average changes from 0.64% to 0.52% because I2P is excluded. Other reported values change, including the SDv1.5 Ring-A-Bell baseline from 71.96% to 98.13% and several ablation ASRs. SDv1.4 sexual-content result columns and Q16 inpainting scores are omitted.

T1.justification: The target-selection construction and Equations (1)–(7) retain their mathematical content under notation changes. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs. The added explanation of loss compatibility introduces no new formal result.

C1.justification: The central claim of robust defense with preserved benign quality and zero inference overhead remains. v2 narrows the headline objective from general NSFW defense to sexual-content mitigation and replaces the prominent plug-and-play contribution framing with explicit compatibility with recent diffusion models.

C2.justification: v2 explains why fixed original nudity vectors and the evolving neutralized vector do not conflict, explicitly acknowledges semantic distortion of benign prompts, and adds cultural-sensitivity discussion. Its I2I interpretation changes from lowest ASR across all scenarios to lowest average ASR. The earlier limitations concerning image-based attacks and closed-source models remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds encoder-specific memory and training times, including T5-XXL CPU offloading with DeepSpeed, batch size 16, and 160 minutes per epoch. Existing software versions and basic training settings remain. v1's explicit DES repository link disappears; v2 instead states that code and data accompany supplementary material, whose availability cannot be verified from these PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 introduces a dedicated sexual-content-mitigation subsection discussing SafeGen and ShieldDiff, adds positioning against GLoCE and EraseAnything, and motivates encoder modification through knowledge localization and continual learning. Additional architecture and image-assessment references further expand the research context beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, terminology, and experimental narrative are substantially revised. UEN, SEP, and PALA terminology becomes simpler loss descriptions. Inpainting results move into the main text, principal ablations move into Appendix D, and the earlier appendices are extensively consolidated and reorganized.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column main-text layout to a single-column layout with wrapped tables and figures. v1 Figures 1–2 become v2 Figure 1, and Figures 8–9 become Figure 6. The overview schematic is simplified, the main qualitative grid is reduced, tables are restructured with colored rankings, and numerous new result displays are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for generalization and benign semantic preservation through newer-model evaluations, another adaptive attack, additional concepts, and direct analysis of semantic damage (Table 7, Section 4.4, Appendix E.1). These gains strengthen the scientific assessment beyond the changed headline averages. They outweigh localized reporting defects: Table 9 gives a negative-prompt average of 78.04% although its entries average 32.78%, and the broad 90-second training claim remains insufficiently qualified despite the much slower T5 training disclosed in Appendix A.
